title: Project: Where Are The Urchins?
text: This data was collected by the CSUMB Rocky Intertidal Lab in 2021 including the percent cover of various algae types and the density of purple sea urchins across 7 sites; Pescadero Point, Carmel Point, Hopkins, China Rock, Sea Palm, Cannery Row. Algae percent cover was estimated by using one meter quadrats and identifying primary algae functional groups and sessile organisms. This analysis was conducted to see if sites have different abundances in algae types and urchin density. Results from this analysis could give us an idea of how different sites may be changing over time with changes in herbivory due to increases in purple sea urchins.

title: Project: Where Are The Urchins?
text:
Data Cleaning
To clean these data I first fixed any spelling errors in sites that caused the same sites to show up multiple times with different spelling by combining them into one label for each site. I then removed all columns I did not need for my analysis. To ensure I could include all algae types in a boxplot, I pivoted the all algae type columns longer into one column for which algae type a percent cover estimate is for called “algae_type” and created a new column for the percent cover estimates called “perc_cover”. Finally, to make sure the algae boxplot showed the full functional group names, not the abbreviations, I changed the abbreviated names of algae groups to the full name.

title: Project: Where Are The Urchins?
text:
Urchin Density
This visualization shows boxplots of the urchin density of seven different sites across the Monterey Bay ordered from lowest urchin density to highest urchin density.Pescadero Point shows the highest urchin density at a median of around 180 individuals recorded, Cannery Row and Carmel Point with 50 and 40 individuals respectively. All other sites had an average number of urchins close to 0. Several sites had transects with especially high outliers and urchin density varies across sites. Looking further into the metadata of these sites and what may be driving these different abundances of urchin could be helpful.





Boxplots showing the urchin density in individuals at each of the sites monitored. Pescadero Point had the highest number of urchins around a 180 median.

title: Project: Where Are The Urchins?
text:
Algae Percent Cover in Monterey
This visualization shows the percent cover of each algae functional group across intertidal zones of Monterey Bay. Similar to the first one it shows the percent cover of each group for all seven of the sites. Each site show a different combination of abundance of various algae groups and some are dominated by different functional groups than others or even by bare rock. Hopkins, China Rock, and Carmel Point are dominated by leathery algae. Cannery Row and Pescadero Point are dominated by bare rock, meaning there is a lack of algae at those sites. Point Pinos and Sea Palm are dominated by Crustose Non-Corraline, then bare rock and leathery algae respectively.
We can see that algae abundance varies quite a bit across sites! Combining this data with urchin density to see if certain algae types tend to persist where urchins are abundant could reveal interesting trends as to how intertidal communities change with increases or decreases in herbivory related to abundance of sea urchins.





Boxplot with site on the x axis and percent cover of algae on the y axis. Color is mapped to algae group. Sites China Rock, Carmel Point, and Hopkins have the highest percent cover of Leathery algae, while Pescadero Point and Cannery Row are dominated by bare rock, and Point Pinos and Sea Palm hae the highest Crustose Non-Coralline percent cover.

title: Portfolio
text:
About this site
Hi! My name is Riley Calbow. I am a fourth year student at California State University Monterey Bay studying marine science and statistics. I participate in undergraduate research on intertidal ecosystems and phycological changes over time. My expected graduation date is fall 2026 and I plan to contribute to the conservation of coastal ecosystems in the near future.

Data Description

Identify your data source.

The Haupt Lab and MARINe/PISCO dataset

Describe your data, including variables and data types.

List of variables in the dataframe:
Site: character
Date: numeric
Transect #: numeric
Latitude and Longitude for start and end transect: numeric
Quadrat #: numeric
Sea or Land Side: character
One column for the percent cover each organism observed: includes various functional groups of algae, kelp, mussels, anemones, barnacles, and other: numeric
Urchin density: numeric
Who entered the Data: character
Notes: character
These datasets include the observed percent cover of various organisms within intertidal sites across the Monterey Peninsula

Identify the research questions you want to answer.

How have both urchin density and algae cover changed over time and how do they appear to have interacted with each other? Has one increased and the other decreased, or vice versa?


Data Visualization

What do you want your final visualizations to look like?

I definitely want to include boxplots of each site to show urchin density. This is part of my preliminary data visualization and analysis for my capstone proposal so ideally I would like to include an NMDs plot which I have some experience with.

What do you want to highlight in your final visualizations in order to answer your research questions? How do you plan to do that?

I’d like to highlight change over time and how different sites have changed. I’d like to just get a general idea of how intertidal ecosystems have changed over time and maybe highlight specific sites that saw large changes. Maybe using colors or ordering my visualizations in a way that draws more attention to them.

What is missing from your data or would need to change in your data to create these visualizations?

I mainly think I will need to join datasets together to create comprehensive visualizations as opposed to several smaller ones.


Data Cleaning
The answer to at least three of these questions should be “YES” for the data to meet the necessary standards to demonstrate your cleaning. Your data source should not be an already perfectly prepared data set.

Do you need to reformat any variables into different types (e.g. factors, time, dates, strings)? Or remove information from variable values?

No

Do you need to deal with any missing data, especially missing data coded other than NA?

No

Do you need to filter your data? How?

Yes, by sites or location and for specific species

Do you need to create any new variables? What variables? How?

Yes, a total percent cover may be helpful for analysis as well as a proportion of percent cover instead of just percent cover

Do you need to add new data (join) to your data? What data? How?

Yes, I have several csvs that will need to be joined together so I can have urchin and algae data in the same csv.

Do you need pivot your data in any way? Why? How?

No

Do you need to summarize any of the variables? Which ones? How?

Yes, urchin and algae percent cover will likely be summarized as a mean proportion for each year we have data

What other aspects of your data need to be “fixed” in order to make your data visualizations?

Last time I used this data many of the site names had different letters capitalized, different abbreviations, etc so names will need to be cleaned.
Most will answer yes to the following for making your programming more efficient using select(), but you should have three other yeses above.

Are there any variables you can exclude from your data?

Yes
